decks.title: Magnetism — Part 1: Induced magnetism and field lines
goals: Explain why a magnet induces magnetism in iron before it attracts it
Draw the field lines of a bar magnet and state their properties
Use field lines to say where a field is strong and which way it points

slides.heading: Magnets and their fields
slides.body_md: Part 1: how a magnet makes iron magnetic before it attracts it, and how the field around a magnet is drawn with field lines.

visual.alt: Flow: magnetic materials, induction, field lines, properties of field lines

slides.narration: This part asks what happens when iron comes near a magnet, and then shows how the invisible field around a magnet is drawn and read.

slides.heading: Magnetic materials and poles
slides.body_md: **Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt** are attracted by a magnet; wood, plastic, copper and glass are not. Every magnet has two poles, **N** and **S**: **like poles repel and unlike poles attract**.

visual.alt: Table of materials attracted and not attracted by a magnet

slides.narration: Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic materials. Wood, plastic, copper and glass are not. Like poles push apart, and unlike poles pull together.

slides.heading: Induced magnetism
slides.body_md: Bring a soft iron bar near the **N pole** of a magnet. The magnet **induces** poles in it: the **nearer end becomes a S pole** and the **far end a N pole**. Unlike poles then attract, so the bar is pulled towards the magnet.

slides.heading: Induction precedes attraction
slides.body_md: A magnet can attract iron **only after** it has made the iron magnetic by induction. An unmagnetised iron piece is attracted too, so **attraction is not a sure test** of a magnet. **Repulsion** is the sure test.

visual.alt: Table comparing a magnet and unmagnetised iron near a pole

slides.narration: Both a magnet and a plain piece of iron are pulled by a magnet. Only a magnet can be pushed away by it. So repulsion is the sure test for a magnet.

slides.heading: Quick check: induced poles
slides.body_md: Think of the end of the nail nearest to the pole.

visual.alt: Table giving the pole of the magnet end near the nail

slides.narration: The north pole of a magnet is brought near the head of an iron nail. What pole is induced at the head?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a chain of nails
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Two iron nails hang one below the other from the N pole of a magnet. Give the poles of each nail and explain why the second nail hangs on.

**Step 1.** Nail 1 is magnetised by the magnet: its upper end is a **S pole** and its lower end a **N pole**.

**Step 2.** Nail 1 now acts as a magnet and magnetises nail 2: the upper end of nail 2 is a **S pole** and the lower end a **N pole**.

**Step 3.** The N end of nail 1 attracts the S end of nail 2.

slides.heading: Field lines of a bar magnet
slides.body_md: A **field line** shows the direction of the magnetic field. Outside the magnet the lines go from the **N pole to the S pole**; inside they go from S to N, so every line is a **closed curve**.

visual.alt: Field lines of a bar magnet from the N pole to the S pole

slides.narration: The lines leave the north pole, curve round and enter the south pole. Inside the magnet they continue from south to north, so each line is a closed loop.

slides.heading: Properties of field lines
slides.body_md: Field lines are **closed curves**, with the **tangent** giving the direction of the field. They **never cross**. They are **crowded where the field is strong** and **far apart where it is weak**.

rows: N to S outside, S to N inside

visual.alt: Table of the properties of field lines and what each means

slides.narration: Lines never cross, because the field has only one direction at a point. Where the lines crowd together the field is strong. Parallel lines that are equally spaced show a uniform field.

slides.heading: Quick check: crossing lines
slides.body_md: How many directions can the field have at one point?

rows: Field lines cross at a point

visual.alt: Table asking whether field lines can cross

slides.narration: Two field lines are drawn crossing each other at a point. Why is this impossible?

slides.heading: Plotting a field line with a compass
slides.body_md: Place a small compass near the N pole. Mark the two ends of the needle, move the compass so that one end sits on the second dot, and repeat. Join the dots and add an arrow. The needle always lies **along the line**.

visual.alt: Compass needles lying along a field line of a bar magnet

slides.narration: The needle of a small compass lies along the field line, with its north end pointing the way the field points. Moving the compass step by step and marking dots draws the line.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: reading a field diagram
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** On a diagram of a bar magnet, which place has the strongest field and which way does a compass needle point just beyond the N pole?

**Step 1.** The lines are most crowded near the **poles**, so the field is strongest there and weakest far away.

**Step 2.** Beyond the N pole the lines point **away from the magnet**, so the N end of the needle points away from the magnet.

visual.alt: Field lines of a bar magnet from the N pole to the S pole

slides.narration: Look for where the lines crowd together, near the poles, for the strongest field. Beyond the north pole the lines point away from the magnet, so the north end of a compass needle points away too.

slides.heading: Quick check: direction at a point
slides.body_md: Outside the magnet the lines run from N to S.

rows: Above the middle of a magnet

visual.alt: Table giving a point above the middle of a bar magnet

slides.narration: A bar magnet has its north pole on the right. A small compass is placed above its middle. Which way does the north end of the needle point?

slides.heading: Quick check: strength of the field
slides.body_md: Where are the lines closest together?

visual.alt: Table of the spacing of field lines near and far from a pole

slides.narration: A diagram shows the field lines of a magnet. Where is the field strongest?

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: A magnet first induces opposite poles in iron (nearer end unlike), then attracts it.
Repulsion, not attraction, is the sure test for a magnet.
Field lines go N to S outside a magnet, never cross, and crowd where the field is strong.
A compass needle lies along a field line.

visual.alt: Summary table of the main facts of Part 1

slides.narration: To sum up. A magnet magnetises iron by induction before it attracts it. Only repulsion proves a magnet. Field lines run from north to south outside, never cross and crowd where the field is strong.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Name the induced poles: the nearer end is the unlike pole.
Always put arrows on field lines, from N to S outside the magnet.
Never draw lines that cross or stop in mid-air.
Use repulsion, not attraction, as the test for a magnet.

visual.alt: Table of a common slip and its fix

slides.narration: Exam tips. Name the induced poles correctly. Draw arrows on every field line. Do not let lines cross. And remember that only repulsion is a sure test for a magnet.

decks.title: Magnetism — Part 2: The earth's field and neutral points
goals: Give evidence for the earth's magnetic field and explain how a compass shows direction
Locate the neutral points of a bar magnet placed with its N pole pointing north and pointing south
Explain why the net field is zero at a neutral point and find the resultant of two fields

slides.heading: The earth as a magnet
slides.body_md: Part 2: the earth's own magnetic field, the compass, and the points near a magnet where the magnet's field and the earth's field cancel.

visual.alt: Flow: the earth as a magnet, the compass, the combined field, neutral points

slides.narration: This part treats the earth as a giant magnet, shows how a compass uses its field, and then finds the special points where a bar magnet and the earth cancel each other.

slides.heading: The earth as a bar magnet
slides.body_md: The earth acts like a huge bar magnet. Its **magnetic S pole is near the geographic north** and its magnetic N pole near the geographic south. The N pole of a compass is attracted to the S pole in the north.

visual.alt: The earth as a bar magnet with compass needles

slides.narration: The earth behaves like a bar magnet whose south pole is near the geographic north. A compass needle, a tiny magnet, lines up with the field, and its north end points towards the geographic north.

slides.heading: Evidence for the earth’s field
slides.body_md: A **freely suspended bar magnet** or a pivoted needle always rests along the **north-south line**. Soft iron left in that line for a long time becomes weakly magnetised. Neutral points exist near magnets.

rows: a second field cancels the magnet’s

visual.alt: Table of evidence for the earth’s magnetic field

slides.narration: A freely hanging magnet always comes to rest pointing north and south. That shows a magnetic field is acting on it everywhere, and the field belongs to the earth.

slides.heading: Quick check: why the needle points north
slides.body_md: Unlike poles attract.

visual.alt: Table asking what the north pole of a needle is attracted to

slides.narration: The north pole of a compass needle points to the geographic north. Why?

slides.heading: The compass and the uniform field
slides.body_md: A **compass** is a small magnetised needle on a pivot; its N pole points roughly **north**. Over a small region, the earth’s field is **uniform**: parallel, equally spaced lines pointing north.

visual.alt: Table of the earth’s field over a small region and over the whole earth

slides.narration: Over a table or a classroom the earth’s field is the same everywhere, with straight parallel lines pointing north. Over the whole earth it changes from place to place.

slides.heading: Neutral points
slides.body_md: Near a bar magnet the field is the **sum** of the magnet’s field and the earth’s uniform field. A **neutral point** is a point where they are **equal and opposite**, so the **resultant field is zero**. A compass there can rest in any direction.

visual.alt: Table describing a neutral point

slides.narration: At a neutral point the magnet pulls one way and the earth pulls the opposite way with the same strength. The two cancel, the resultant field is zero, and a compass needle there is not turned at all.

slides.heading: N pole pointing north
slides.body_md: With the magnet’s **N pole pointing north**, its field on the **equatorial line** points south, against the earth’s field. The **two neutral points are on the equatorial line**, one on each side.

visual.alt: Combined field with the N pole of the magnet pointing north and two neutral points on the equatorial line

slides.narration: With the north pole of the magnet pointing north, the field of the magnet on the line through its middle, at right angles to its length, points south. It opposes the earth, so the neutral points lie there, east and west of the magnet.

slides.heading: N pole pointing south
slides.body_md: With the magnet’s **N pole pointing south**, its field on the **axial line** points south, against the earth’s field. The **two neutral points are on the axial line**, one beyond each pole.

visual.alt: Combined field with the N pole of the magnet pointing south and two neutral points on the axial line

slides.narration: Turn the magnet round so that its north pole points south. Now the field of the magnet along its length opposes the earth, so the neutral points lie on that line, one beyond each end of the magnet.

slides.heading: Quick check: where are the neutral points?
slides.body_md: N pole pointing north: look at the line at right angles to the magnet.

visual.alt: Table giving the direction of the N pole of a bar magnet

slides.narration: A bar magnet is placed with its north pole pointing north. On which line do its neutral points lie?

slides.heading: Quick check: the other way round
slides.body_md: N pole pointing south: look along the length of the magnet.

visual.alt: Table giving the direction of the N pole of a bar magnet

slides.narration: The magnet is turned so that its north pole points south. On which line do its neutral points lie?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: distance of a neutral point from a pole
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A neutral point lies on the equatorial line, 8 cm from the centre of a 12 cm magnet. Find its distance from each pole. (The poles are taken at the ends.)

**Step 1.** Each pole is 6 cm from the centre, at right angles to the line to the neutral point.

**Step 2.** $d = \sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ cm.

visual.alt: Table of the lengths in the neutral point problem

slides.narration: The neutral point, the centre and a pole form a right angled triangle. Six and eight give a hypotenuse of ten, so the neutral point is ten centimetres from each pole.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the direction of a compass needle
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** At a point the earth's field is 3 units north and a magnet's field is 4 units east. Find the resultant field.

**Step 1.** The fields are at right angles, so $R = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$ units.

**Step 2.** The angle from north is $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{4}{3} \approx 53^\circ$ towards the east. A compass lies along this direction.

notes.title: Magnetism — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Induced magnetism: induction precedes attraction
sections.body_md:
**Magnetic materials** (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt) are attracted by a magnet; wood, plastic, copper and glass are not.

When a piece of **soft iron** is brought near the N pole of a magnet, the magnet first **induces** magnetism in it: the end **nearer** the N pole becomes a **S pole** and the **far** end becomes a **N pole**. Because unlike poles attract and the nearer pole is the stronger, the iron is then **attracted**. So **induction precedes attraction**: a magnet can attract only after it has magnetised the iron. A second nail hanging from the first is held in the same way, each nail being magnetised by the one above it.

Soft iron loses its magnetism when the magnet is taken away (a temporary magnet); steel keeps it (a permanent magnet).

Since an unmagnetised iron piece is also attracted, **attraction is not a sure test** for a magnet. **Repulsion is the sure test**: only a magnet can repel the pole of a magnet.

key_terms.definition_md: The magnetism produced in a piece of magnetic material when it is placed near a magnet.
Repulsion: only a magnet repels the like pole of another magnet.

sections.heading: 2. Magnetic field lines and their properties
sections.body_md:
The space around a magnet in which its magnetic effect is felt is its **magnetic field**. A **field line** is the path that a free N pole would follow. A small **compass needle** placed at a point lies along the line through that point, its N pole pointing the way the field points.

**Properties of field lines**
- They start from the **N pole** and end at the **S pole** outside the magnet; inside the magnet they run from S to N, so each line is a **closed curve**.
- The **tangent** to a line at a point gives the direction of the field there.
- Lines **never cross**; if they did, the field would have two directions at one point.
- Lines are **crowded where the field is strong** (near the poles) and **far apart where it is weak**. Parallel, equally spaced lines show a **uniform** field.

To plot a line, a compass is moved step by step: mark the positions of the two ends of the needle, join the dots and add an arrow from N to S.

A line whose tangent at any point gives the direction of the magnetic field there.

sections.heading: 3. The earth's magnetic field and the compass
sections.body_md:
The earth behaves like a **huge bar magnet**. Its **magnetic S pole is near the geographic north** and its magnetic N pole near the geographic south; that is why the N pole of a magnet points towards the north (unlike poles attract).

**Evidence** that the earth has a magnetic field: a freely suspended bar magnet or a pivoted compass needle always comes to rest pointing along the same north-south line; a piece of soft iron left pointing north-south for a long time becomes weakly magnetised; neutral points exist near a bar magnet.

A **magnetic compass** is a small magnetised needle on a pivot. Its **N pole points to the geographic north** (roughly), so it shows direction. Over a small region such as a table, the **earth's field is uniform**: it has parallel, equally spaced lines along the north-south direction, pointing north. (The line along which a compass rests is called the magnetic meridian; it differs a little from the geographic one in most places.)

key_terms.definition_md: A small magnetised needle pivoted at its centre; its N pole points roughly to the geographic north.
The magnetic S pole is near the geographic north and the magnetic N pole near the geographic south.

sections.heading: 4. Combined field of a bar magnet and the earth: neutral points
sections.body_md:
Near a bar magnet the field is the sum of the field of the magnet and the **uniform field of the earth**. A **neutral point** is a point where these two fields are **equal in size and opposite in direction**, so the **resultant field is zero**. A compass placed there is not turned by any field and can rest pointing in any direction.

- **N pole of the magnet pointing north:** the magnet's field on its **equatorial line** (the perpendicular bisector) points south, opposite to the earth's field, so the two **neutral points lie on the equatorial line**, one on the east side and one on the west side.
- **N pole of the magnet pointing south:** on the **axial line** the magnet's field also points south, opposing the earth's field there, so the two **neutral points lie on the axial line**, one beyond each pole.

A **stronger magnet has its neutral points farther away**, because its field is still as strong as the earth's at a greater distance.

**Directions:** where two fields at right angles act together, a compass lies along their resultant. If the earth's field is 3 units north and the magnet's is 4 units east, the resultant is 5 units, 53° east of north; if the two are equal the needle lies at 45°. **Distances** (the magnet's poles are a little inside its ends): a neutral point 8 cm from the centre of a 12 cm magnet, on the equatorial line, is 10 cm from each pole.

key_terms.definition_md: A point where the magnetic field of a magnet is equal and opposite to the earth’s field, so the resultant field is zero.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying that a magnet attracts iron "because iron is a magnet"; the iron is first magnetised by induction, with the nearer end an unlike pole.
- Taking attraction as proof that a bar is a magnet; only repulsion is a sure test.
- Drawing field lines that cross, that have no arrows, or that point from S to N outside the magnet.
- Calling the earth's pole in the north its "magnetic north pole"; it is a magnetic S pole (that is why the N pole of a compass points to it).
- Putting the neutral points on the wrong line: N pole pointing north gives points on the equatorial line; N pole pointing south gives points on the axial line.
- Forgetting that the resultant field is zero at a neutral point, not just small.
- Giving distances from the centre when the question asks for the distance from a pole (the poles are a little inside the ends).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, a pole or a direction.
- 2 marks: two properties or a short reason; a numerical on distances or directions.
- 3 marks: a description (plotting a line) or a reason with a diagram.
- 10-mark structured question: a lettered field diagram or neutral-point diagram: name poles, give directions, locate points, one numerical and a reason.
